Indian heritage

Classical dances of India: the eight forms and their states

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

India has eight classical dance forms recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (north India), Kathakali and Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur) and Sattriya (Assam). All trace their theory to the Natya Shastra and combine pure dance, expressive storytelling and music.

Talaash Heritage runs a lecture on temple sculpture and iconography that shows dancers and musicians carved in stone, for schools, colleges and dance students.

What makes a dance classical in India?

In the Indian sense, a classical dance is one with a codified grammar, a long teacher to student lineage, and a theoretical base in old treatises, above all the Natya Shastra attributed to Bharata. That Sanskrit text on drama, usually dated somewhere between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, sets out ideas still used in every classical form: rasa (the aesthetic mood an audience tastes), bhava (the emotion the performer expresses) and abhinaya (the means of expression).

Three elements recur. Nritta is pure dance, rhythmic movement with no story. Nritya adds expression, with hand gestures (mudras), face and eyes conveying meaning. Natya is dramatic performance. Different forms weight these differently: Kathakali leans towards drama, while a Kathak recital can spend long stretches on rhythmic footwork.

List of the 8 classical dances of India and their states

The Sangeet Natak Akademi, India's national academy for music, dance and drama, recognises eight forms. The Ministry of Culture has at times also listed Chhau, which is why some books say nine.

DanceState or regionDistinctive features
BharatanatyamTamil NaduHalf-seated stance (aramandi), crisp geometric lines, sculptural poses; grew from the temple and court dance of Tamil country
KathakNorth India (Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan)Fast footwork with ankle bells, spins (chakkar), storytelling; shaped in temple, Mughal and Rajput courts; Lucknow, Jaipur and Banaras gharanas
KathakaliKeralaDance drama with elaborate green and red make-up, large headdresses, epic stories; traditionally all-male, performed through the night
MohiniyattamKeralaGentle swaying movements, white and gold costume, solo female dance
KuchipudiAndhra PradeshNamed after a village in Krishna district; quick, fluid movements, dance on the rim of a brass plate in some items
OdissiOdishaTribhanga (three-bend) posture, square chauka stance; links to the sculpture of Odisha's temples
ManipuriManipurSoft, rounded movements, no ankle bells, barrel-shaped skirts in Ras Lila; deeply tied to Vaishnava devotion
SattriyaAssamCreated in the sattras (monasteries) founded by the saint Srimanta Sankardev in the 15th and 16th centuries; recognised as classical in 2000

Origins: temples, courts and the Natya Shastra

Indian classical dance has deep roots, but the forms seen on stage today were largely shaped in the last few centuries and then reconstructed and renamed in the twentieth century. Sculpture is one of the best sources for earlier dance. Temple walls at Chidambaram, Konark and Khajuraho show dancers and musicians, and the karanas (dance units) of the Natya Shastra are carved on some south Indian temples. Learning to read temple sculpture makes these panels come alive.

Many forms were performed by hereditary communities attached to temples and courts. Colonial-era laws and social reform movements in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries pushed these communities out, and revivalists such as Rukmini Devi Arundale (Bharatanatyam) and the poet Vallathol Narayana Menon, who founded Kerala Kalamandalam in 1930, rebuilt the forms for the concert stage. Historians now study both the continuity and the reinvention.

Classical dance and Indian heritage

Classical dance is a clear case of intangible cultural heritage: it lives only in the bodies of dancers and their teachers. Kutiyattam, the Sanskrit theatre of Kerala closely related to Kathakali's world, is on UNESCO's intangible list, as are Chhau and Manipur's Sankirtana.

The forms also connect to places you can visit. Bharatanatyam's stance is visible on Chola temple walls, and Odissi poses repeat on the temples of Bhubaneswar and Konark, which our journey through the temples of eastern India explores. For a wider view of the folk side, see our guide to folk dances of India state-wise.

Music is inseparable from all eight forms. Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi and Mohiniyattam are danced to Carnatic music, while Kathak and Odissi use Hindustani or regional music. Each form also has its own costume, jewellery and make-up conventions, many of them recorded in paintings and old photographs, which makes dance history a field that draws on art, texts and living memory together.

Classical dances of India: notes for students

  • Number recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi: eight.
  • Key text: Natya Shastra, attributed to Bharata.
  • Three elements: nritta (pure dance), nritya (expressive dance), natya (drama).
  • Kerala has two forms: Kathakali and Mohiniyattam.
  • Newest addition: Sattriya of Assam, recognised in 2000.
  • Form most shaped by Mughal and Rajput courts: Kathak.
  • Tribhanga posture: Odissi. Aramandi stance: Bharatanatyam.

Questions people ask

How many classical dances are there in India?

The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises eight classical dances: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Mohiniyattam, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri and Sattriya. Some sources list nine because the Ministry of Culture has also included Chhau, a martial dance from eastern India.

Which is the oldest classical dance of India?

There is no single agreed answer. Bharatanatyam and Odissi are often called the oldest because temple sculpture links them to dance traditions many centuries old. But all present-day forms were reshaped in the twentieth century, so claims of age need care.

Which state has two classical dances?

Kerala. Both Kathakali, the dramatic dance with elaborate make-up, and Mohiniyattam, a graceful solo dance, come from Kerala. Kutiyattam, the Sanskrit theatre form, also comes from Kerala, though it is classed as theatre.

Which classical dance is from Assam?

Sattriya. It developed in the sattras, the Vaishnava monasteries of Assam founded after the saint Srimanta Sankardev, and was performed by monks. The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised it as a classical dance in 2000, making it the most recent addition.

What is the Natya Shastra?

The Natya Shastra is an old Sanskrit treatise on drama, dance and music, attributed to Bharata and usually dated to somewhere around 200 BCE to 200 CE. It defines ideas such as rasa and bhava that remain the theoretical base of Indian classical dance.
